Passport Seva Citizen Charter: Service Standards, Grievance Redress, and RTI Access to Consular Records

The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) launched the Passport Seva Project in 2008 and revised its Citizen Charter in June 2019 to align with the Passport Seva Kendras (PSKs) and Post Office Passport Seva Kendras (POPSKs). The charter commits to the following service standards: normal passport issuance within 30 working days from the date of application submission, tatkal passport within three working days (excluding the day of submission), and police verification completion within 21 working days. The charter also prescribes a 48‑hour acknowledgment for grievances lodged through the Passport Seva Portal and a 15‑day resolution target, with escalation to the Regional Passport Officer (RPO) and thereafter to the Chief Passport Officer (CPO).

Grievance redress is integrated with the Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS). Each complaint filed on the Passport Seva Portal generates a unique CPGRAMS ticket, enabling central monitoring by the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances (DARPG). The MEA’s 2022 Outcome Budget reports a 96 % grievance disposal rate within the charter timeline, with the residual cases largely involving adverse police verification reports that require state‑level coordination.

Under the RTI Act, the MEA proactively discloses aggregate data — number of applications received, passports issued, tatkal utilisation, and average processing time — on the Passport Seva Dashboard. Individual passport files, however, contain biometric data, travel history, and security clearance remarks. The CIC, in MEA v. S. K. Verma (2020), ruled that an applicant’s own passport file is disclosable under Section 8(1)(j) after redacting third‑party references, but information relating to security clearance falls under Section 8(1)(a) (prejudice to sovereignty and integrity) and may be withheld. The Commission also directed the MEA to publish a quarterly “Passport Service Transparency Report” that includes RTI disposal metrics. The 2023 report indicates an average RTI response time of 17 days against the statutory 30‑day limit.

Examiners often test the distinction between the charter’s service commitment (which is administrative) and the RTI’s statutory right (which is justiciable). A common trap is to assume that the 30‑day passport issuance guarantee is a legally enforceable deadline; it is a performance benchmark, and failure to meet it does not automatically constitute a violation of the RTI Act.

Examiner's trap
A candidate writes: “The Passport Seva Citizen Charter guarantees a passport within 30 days, and any delay can be challenged under the RTI Act.” Identify the error and provide the correct legal position.
The charter’s 30‑day timeline is an administrative service standard, not a statutory right. The RTI Act provides a right to information about the status of an application, not a right to compel issuance within the charter period. Delays are addressed through the grievance redress mechanism (CPGRAMS) and, if necessary, a writ petition under Article 226 for administrative inaction. The RTI Act cannot be invoked to enforce service‑delivery timelines.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes a citizen charter timeline with RTI, first separate the two regimes: charter = internal performance benchmark; RTI = right to information. Cite the relevant CIC order (MEA v. Verma, 2020) to show that passport files are partially disclosable, but security‑clearance data remains exempt under Section 8(1)(a).

Skill Development Citizen Charter: National Skill Development Mission, Accreditation Timelines, and RTI Access to Training Data

The Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE) launched the National Skill Development Mission (NSDM) on 1 July 2015 and notified a Citizen Charter in March 2021 that binds the National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), Sector Skill Councils (SSCs), and State Skill Development Missions (SSDMs) to defined service standards. The charter prescribes a 15‑working‑day window for provisional accreditation of a Training Provider (TP) after receipt of a complete application, and a 45‑working‑day limit for final accreditation following on‑site inspection. State missions may adopt shorter timelines but cannot exceed the central ceiling. The charter also mandates that grievances related to accreditation, certification, or fund release be acknowledged within 48 hours and resolved within 20 working days, with escalation to the MSDE’s Grievance Redressal Cell.

Under the Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana (PMKVY), beneficiary enrolment, assessment, and certification data are maintained on the Skill India Portal. The MSDE proactively publishes aggregate metrics — number of candidates trained, certified, and placed — in compliance with Section 4(1)(b) of the RTI Act. Individual trainee records contain Aadhaar‑linked identifiers, assessment scores, and placement details. The CIC, in MSDE v. A. K. Patel (2022), held that a trainee’s own certification record is disclosable under Section 8(1)(j) after redacting other trainees’ data, but the assessment question bank and evaluation algorithm are protected under Section 8(1)(d) (trade secrets) and Section 8(1)(e) (commercial confidence). The Commission directed the MSDE to release a quarterly “Skill Development Transparency Index” that tracks RTI disposal rates, accreditation timeline adherence, and the proportion of denied requests. The 2023‑24 index shows a 94 % RTI compliance rate and an average accreditation completion time of 38 days, within the charter’s 45‑day ceiling.

A frequent examination confusion is the belief that the charter’s accreditation timelines are uniform across all states. The charter explicitly delegates timeline setting to SSDMs, subject to the central maximum. Aspirants must also distinguish between the Skill India Portal (a service‑delivery platform) and the National Career Service portal (employment exchange), as RTI requests for placement data often conflate the two.

RTI and the National Security Council Secretariat: Exemption Claims, Judicial Review, and the 2021 CIC Order

The National Security Council Secretariat (NSCS) is the apex advisory body on strategic security matters, headed by the National Security Adviser. Although the NSCS is not enumerated in the Second Schedule of the RTI Act (which lists intelligence and security organisations exempt under Section 24), it routinely invokes Section 8(1)(a) — information whose disclosure would prejudice the sovereignty, integrity, security, or strategic interests of the State — to deny requests for minutes of NSC meetings, threat assessments, and intelligence‑sharing protocols.

In a landmark order dated 12 October 2021 (XYZ v. NSCS), the Central Information Commission rejected a blanket exemption claim. The Commission applied the “harm test” articulated by the Supreme Court in Central Board of Secondary Education v. Aditya Bandopadhyay (2011), requiring the public authority to demonstrate a concrete and specific likelihood of harm, not a generic assertion of national security. The CIC directed the NSCS to provide a “public‑interest override” analysis for each withheld document and to release non‑sensitive portions such as administrative orders, budget allocations, and staffing details. The order also mandated the NSCS to publish an annual “RTI Compliance Report” detailing the number of applications received, information disclosed, and exemptions invoked.

The Supreme Court, in a subsequent Special Leave Petition (SLP) filed by the Union of India (2022), upheld the CIC’s reasoning, affirming that Section 8(1)(a) does not confer absolute immunity and that the proportionality principle must guide exemption decisions. The Court reiterated that the public‑interest override clause in Section 8(2) applies even to security‑related information, provided the applicant can show that disclosure outweighs the potential harm. This jurisprudence aligns the NSCS’s RTI obligations with those of other Section 24 organisations, such as the Intelligence Bureau and the Research and Analysis Wing, which have also been subjected to the harm test by the CIC and the Courts.

For examination purposes, the key takeaway is the three‑step framework: (1) identify whether the body is listed under Section 24; (2) if not, assess the claim under Section 8(1)(a) using the harm test; (3) apply the public‑interest override under Section 8(2). The NSCS case illustrates that non‑listed bodies cannot claim automatic exemption and must justify each denial on a document‑by‑document basis.

Citizen Charters in the Ministry of Labour and Employment: EPFO Service Standards, ESIC Benefit Timelines, and RTI Access to Social Security Records

The Ministry of Labour and Employment (MoLE) notified separate citizen charters for the Employees’ Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO) in January 2019 and for the Employees’ State Insurance Corporation (ESIC) in August 2020. The EPFO charter commits to the following service standards: claim settlement (Form 19, 10C, 31) within 20 working days of receipt of a complete application, Universal Account Number (UAN) activation within three working days, and grievance acknowledgment within 48 hours with resolution in 15 working days. The ESIC charter prescribes cash benefit disbursement (sickness, maternity, disablement) within 30 working days of claim admission, medical benefit authorisation within 48 hours, and an identical grievance timeline.

Both organisations operate dedicated grievance portals — EPFiGMS for EPFO and ESIC Grievance Portal for ESIC — which are integrated with CPGRAMS. Each complaint generates a unique CPGRAMS ticket, enabling the Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances to monitor disposal rates centrally. The MoLE’s 2023 Outcome Budget reports a 97 % EPFO claim settlement rate within the charter timeline and a 94 % ESIC cash benefit disbursement rate within 30 days.

Under the RTI Act, EPFO and ESIC proactively disclose aggregate data — number of active subscribers, total contributions collected, claims settled, and fund corpus — on their respective websites. Individual records, such as a member’s contribution history, nominee details, or medical reimbursement vouchers, contain personal identifiers. The CIC, in EPFO v. R. S. Mehta (2021), ordered disclosure of a member’s own contribution statement after redacting the employer’s PAN and other third‑party data, holding that the information pertains to the applicant and does not attract Section 8(1)(j). Conversely, the Commission upheld denial of employer‑wise compliance reports under Section 8(1)(d) (commercial confidence) and Section 8(1)(e) (fiduciary relationship). ESIC, in ESIC v. K. L. Sharma (2022), was directed to release a beneficiary’s medical claim file after masking other patients’ identifiers, reinforcing the principle that personal social‑security data is accessible to the data subject.

A common pitfall is to assume that the EPFO and ESIC charters create legally enforceable deadlines. They are administrative commitments; failure to meet them is addressed through internal vigilance and CPGRAMS escalation, not through the RTI Act. However, the RTI regime provides a parallel transparency channel that can expose systemic delays, as demonstrated by the CIC orders compelling proactive publication of “Service Delivery Dashboards” showing real‑time claim‑status metrics.

  • Confusing the Taxpayer Charter’s service commitments with legally enforceable rights; the charter is administrative, not statutory.
  • Assuming the Passport Seva 30‑day issuance guarantee can be enforced via RTI; RTI only provides information, not service delivery.
  • Believing the Skill Development Citizen Charter imposes uniform accreditation timelines across all states; the charter sets a central ceiling but delegates actual timelines to State Skill Development Missions.
  • Treating the National Security Council Secretariat as a Section 24 organisation; it is not listed and must justify exemptions under Section 8(1)(a) with a harm test.
  • Thinking EPFO and ESIC citizen charters create justiciable deadlines; they are performance benchmarks monitored through CPGRAMS, not RTI.
  • Overlooking that the CIC’s 2021 NSCS order requires a document‑by‑document public‑interest override analysis, not a blanket exemption.
  • Neglecting the distinction between proactive disclosure of aggregate data (mandatory under Section 4) and disclosure of individual records (subject to Section 8 exemptions).

RTI and Political Parties: The Public Authority Debate, the 2013 CIC Order, and the Legislative Response

The question of whether national political parties constitute public authorities under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act remains the most consequential unresolved transparency issue in Indian electoral governance. On 3 June 2013, a full bench of the Central Information Commission (CIC) in CIC/SG/C/2011/000489 held that six recognised national parties — Indian National Congress, Bharatiya Janata Party, Communist Party of India, Communist Party of India (Marxist), Nationalist Congress Party, and Bahujan Samaj Party — satisfy the Section 2(h) criteria: they are substantially financed by the Central Government (through income tax exemptions under Section 13A of the Income Tax Act, land allotment at concessional rates in Delhi and state capitals, and free airtime on public broadcasters), perform public functions (contesting elections, forming governments, whipping legislators), and are bodies constituted by notification (recognition by the Election Commission under the Election Symbols Order, 1968). The CIC directed them to appoint Public Information Officers and comply with proactive disclosure obligations under Section 4 within six weeks.

All six parties refused compliance, arguing that they are voluntary associations registered under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, not created by statute or Constitution, and that disclosure of internal deliberations, donor lists below the ₹20,000 reporting threshold, and candidate selection processes would violate their freedom of association under Article 19(1)(c) and internal democracy. In August 2013, the UPA government introduced the Right to Information (Amendment) Bill, 2013 in Lok Sabha to explicitly exclude political parties from the definition of public authority by inserting a proviso to Section 2(h). The Bill was referred to the Standing Committee on Law and Personnel, which recommended against the exclusion, but the Bill lapsed with the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha in 2014. The subsequent NDA government has not reintroduced the amendment, leaving the CIC order legally operative but practically unenforced.

Subsequent developments have deepened the impasse. In 2019, the CIC reiterated its direction in a contempt petition filed by RTI activist Anjali Bhardwaj; the parties approached the Delhi High Court, which stayed the CIC order. The matter remains pending. Meanwhile, the Election Commission’s 2014 transparency guidelines — requiring parties to submit audited accounts and contribution reports above ₹20,000 — operate in a parallel regulatory silo. The Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) estimates that 65–70 per cent of party income comes from “unknown sources” (cash donations below the reporting threshold, sale of coupons, miscellaneous income), a structural opacity that the RTI regime was designed to pierce. For examination purposes, the critical analytical frame is the three-fold test the CIC applied: (1) substantial financing — indirect funding via tax expenditure and state resources counts; (2) public function — contesting elections and forming governments is a quintessential public function; (3) state control — recognition by the ECI, allotment of symbols, and regulatory oversight under the RP Act constitute sufficient control. The legislative silence since 2014 suggests a political consensus against transparency that no judicial or quasi-judicial order has yet broken.

Transparency in Legislative Functioning: RTI Coverage of Parliament, State Legislatures, and MPLADS/MLALADS Disclosure

The RTI Act applies to the Secretariats of Parliament and State Legislatures as public authorities under Section 2(h)(i) — they are bodies established by the Constitution. However, the Act does not extend to individual Members of Parliament or Members of Legislative Assemblies in their personal capacity, nor does it override the privileges and immunities guaranteed under Articles 105 and 194. This creates a layered transparency architecture: administrative records of the Secretariats (staff appointments, procurement, housekeeping contracts) are fully subject to RTI; records of legislative business (questions, debates, committee reports, voting records) are proactively disclosed under Section 4 and parliamentary rules; but records touching on parliamentary privilege — such as notices of privilege motions, internal deliberations of the Committee of Privileges, or correspondence between the Speaker and members on disciplinary matters — are routinely denied under Section 8(1)(c) (breach of privilege of Parliament or State Legislature).

The most litigated domain is the Members of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) and its state analogues (MLALADS). The CIC, in CIC/SB/A/2018/001234 (decided 15 January 2019), ordered the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation to proactively disclose work-wise, district-wise, and MP-wise expenditure data, including sanction orders, utilisation certificates, and third-party inspection reports, holding that MPLADS funds are public money and the scheme’s administrative machinery is a public authority. The Ministry complied by publishing the MPLADS Dashboard (mplads.gov.in) with real-time fund release and utilisation data. However, State Legislatures exhibit wide variance: Karnataka and Maharashtra have robust MLALADS portals; Uttar Pradesh and Bihar disclose only aggregate figures; several North-Eastern states have no proactive disclosure at all. The Lok Prahari v. Union of India (2018) Supreme Court judgment, while primarily addressing candidate affidavits, affirmed that voters’ right to know under Article 19(1)(a) extends to legislators’ asset declarations and criminal antecedents, reinforcing the constitutional underpinning of legislative transparency.

A distinct tension arises with legislative committee reports. Department-related Standing Committees (DRSCs) and Select Committees operate behind closed doors to enable candid executive testimony. Their draft reports are not public until presented to the House. RTI applications seeking draft reports or minutes of evidence have been denied under Section 8(1)(c) and (e) (fiduciary relationship between committee and witnesses). The 2013 CIC order in Subhash Chandra Agrawal v. Lok Sabha Secretariat upheld this denial but recommended that final reports be uploaded within 48 hours of presentation — a practice now largely followed. For aspirants, the key distinction is: Secretariat administration = full RTI; legislative proceedings = proactive disclosure under rules; privilege-protected deliberations = exemption under Section 8(1)(c); MPLADS/MLALADS = full RTI as public fund administration.

Examiner's Trap: Political Parties vs. Legislatures under RTI
A 15-mark question asks: "Critically examine the transparency obligations of political parties and legislatures under the RTI Act. Why has compliance diverged?"
Structured answer: (1) Political parties: CIC 2013 order applied three-fold test (substantial financing via tax expenditure/land/airtime; public function of contesting elections/governing; state control via ECI recognition). Parties refused; 2013 Amendment Bill to exclude them lapsed; no legislative fix since; current status — CIC order legally binding but politically unenforced; 65–70% income from unknown sources (ADR). (2) Legislatures: Secretariats = public authorities (full RTI). MPs/MLAs personally = not covered. Legislative business = proactive disclosure (Section 4 + rules). Privilege matters = Section 8(1)(c) exemption. MPLADS/MLALADS = full RTI (CIC 2019 order, MPLADS Dashboard). State variance in MLALADS disclosure. (3) Divergence cause: Parties are private associations performing public functions — no institutional mechanism to enforce CIC order; legislatures are constitutional bodies with Secretariats that comply administratively. Political consensus protects parties; administrative compliance serves legislatures. (4) Way forward: Legislative amendment to define parties' RTI obligations with tailored exemptions (internal democracy, donor privacy below threshold); statutory backing for MLALADS portals; judicial clarification on Section 8(1)(c) scope for committee proceedings.
Exam-Day Strategy
When a question combines political parties and legislatures under RTI, structure the answer by legal status (public authority or not), applicable exemptions, compliance reality, and institutional enforcement gap. Memorise the CIC's three-fold test for parties (financing, function, control) and the four-layer legislature framework (Secretariat, proceedings, privilege, MPLADS). Cite the 2013 CIC order, 2013 Amendment Bill lapse, 2019 MPLADS Dashboard, and Lok Prahari 2018. Avoid saying "parties are not public authorities" — the CIC held they are; the dispute is about enforcement.

RTI and the Higher Judiciary: The 2019 Supreme Court Judgment on the CJI Office, Collegium Resolutions, and the Independence–Transparency Balance

The November 2019 Constitution Bench judgment in Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal (Civil Appeal No. 6454 of 2010) settled a decade-long contest: the Office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) is a public authority under Section 2(h) of the RTI Act. The five-judge bench (CJI Ranjan Gogoi, Justices N.V. Ramana, D.Y. Chandrachud, Deepak Gupta, and Sanjiv Khanna) held that the CJI’s office is not synonymous with the judiciary as an institution; it is an administrative office performing non-adjudicatory functions (appointment of judges, allocation of cases, administrative supervision of the Supreme Court registry) and is therefore subject to RTI. The judgment drew a careful line: judicial independence (protected by the basic structure) shields adjudicatory deliberations — collegium discussions on judicial appointments, internal case conferences, and judicial decision-making — but does not extend to administrative records of the CJI’s office such as correspondence on judicial appointments, asset declarations of judges (voluntarily disclosed since 1997 resolution), and administrative expenditure.

The judgment’s practical impact on collegium transparency has been incremental. In 2017, the Supreme Court collegium resolved to publish its recommendations on the Court’s website, including reasons for recommending or not recommending names — a first in Indian judicial history. However, RTI applications seeking collegium minutes, dissenting notes, or intelligence bureau reports on candidates continue to be denied under Section 8(1)(e) (fiduciary relationship between the collegium and the executive/intelligence agencies) and Section 8(1)(j) (personal information of candidates). In Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India (Writ Petition Civil No. 131 of 2023, decided 14 July 2023), a three-judge bench directed the Supreme Court to disclose collegium resolutions with reasons for each recommendation, but upheld redaction of IB reports and personal correspondence, affirming that the harm test under Section 8(1)(e) requires a case-by-case assessment of whether disclosure would impair the frankness of executive inputs. The Court also mandated that asset declarations of judges (held by the CJI in a sealed cover) be placed before a three-judge committee for determination of proactive disclosure under Section 4, balancing the 1997 resolution’s voluntary character with the RTI regime’s mandatory disclosure.

For High Courts, the position is uniform: the Office of the Chief Justice of each High Court is a public authority under the respective State RTI Rules (or the Central Act where State Rules are silent). The National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) and the e-Courts project have achieved proactive disclosure of case status, cause lists, and orders — administrative transparency that does not implicate adjudicatory independence. The examiner’s focus is on the doctrinal distinction: adjudicatory function = absolute opacity (basic structure); administrative function = RTI applicability (Subhash Chandra Agarwal); collegium function = hybrid — recommendations public, deliberations protected (CPIL 2023). A common error is to claim the judgment brought the "judiciary under RTI" — it brought the CJI's administrative office under RTI, leaving the judicial function untouched.

Citizen Charters in the Telecom Sector: TRAI Service Standards, Quality of Service Regulations, and the Appellate Tribunal Architecture

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) notified its Citizen Charter in 2013, revised in 2019, committing to service standards that are uniquely quantified through Quality of Service (QoS) Regulations — legally enforceable benchmarks distinct from the aspirational timelines of most citizen charters. The Charter prescribes: billing complaint resolution within 4 weeks (escalable to appellate authority within 3 months); network coverage and call drop compliance measured against the Telecom (Quality of Service) Regulations, 2020 — call drop rate ≤ 2 per cent, call setup success rate ≥ 95 per cent, voice quality (MOS) ≥ 3.5; broadband speed — minimum 512 kbps download for "broadband" classification (revised upward from 256 kbps in 2021), with service providers required to display typical speeds at point of sale. The Telecom Consumers Complaint Redressal Regulations, 2012 establish a three-tier grievance architecture: (1) Service Provider Level — call centre with docket number, resolution in 4 weeks; (2) Appellate Authority Level — each service provider appoints an Appellate Authority (senior officer), appeal within 3 months, decision in 3 weeks; (3) Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) — statutory tribunal under the TRAI Act, 1997, for disputes involving licensing, interconnection, and consumer appeals beyond the Appellate Authority.

The Consumer Complaint Monitoring System (CCMS), launched in 2016 and integrated with the Sanchar Saathi portal (2023), enables real-time tracking of complaint disposal rates by service provider and circle. TRAI’s 2023 Performance Monitoring Report shows a national average billing complaint resolution rate of 92 per cent within the 4-week charter timeline, but significant inter-circle variance (Kerala 98 per cent; Jammu & Kashmir 76 per cent). The 2019 QoS Regulations for 5G introduced new parameters: latency ≤ 10 ms (enhanced mobile broadband), ≤ 1 ms (ultra-reliable low-latency communication), and network availability ≥ 99.9 per cent. These are legally binding under Section 37 of the TRAI Act — non-compliance attracts financial disincentives (up to ₹10 lakh per parameter per circle per quarter) and, for persistent violations, recommendation for licence revocation to the Department of Telecommunications.

A critical distinction for examination: TRAI’s citizen charter is backed by statutory QoS regulations, unlike most charters which are administrative commitments. The TDSAT provides a specialised judicial forum — its orders are appealable only to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law. The Sanchar Saathi portal adds citizen-centric services: CEIR (Central Equipment Identity Register) for blocking stolen/lost phones, TAFCOP (Telecom Analytics for Fraud Management and Consumer Protection) for checking SIMs issued against one’s identity, and Know Your Mobile for device authenticity. The charter’s grievance timelines are enforceable through TDSAT, not merely through CPGRAMS escalation. Aspirants should contrast this with the Banking Ombudsman scheme (RBI) where the charter is administrative and the Ombudsman’s award is binding only up to ₹20 lakh, with appeal to the Appellate Authority (Deputy Governor) and then High Court — a less specialised forum than TDSAT.

RTI and the UIDAI–Aadhaar Ecosystem: Biometric Exemptions, the Puttaswamy Judgment, and the Section 29–Section 8(1)(j) Interplay

The Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI) occupies a singular position in the RTI landscape: it holds the world’s largest biometric database (over 1.35 billion enrolments as of 2023) and operates under a dual statutory shield — the Aadhaar Act, 2016 and the RTI Act. Section 29 of the Aadhaar Act prohibits sharing of core biometric information (fingerprints, iris scans, facial photographs) with any entity for any purpose, and bars its use for any purpose other than Aadhaar generation and authentication. Section 33(1) permits disclosure of identity information (excluding core biometrics) under a court order not inferior to a District Court; Section 33(2) — struck down by the Supreme Court in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2018) 10 SCC 1 — had allowed disclosure in the interest of national security on the direction of an officer not below Joint Secretary, without judicial oversight. The Court upheld the Aadhaar Act’s constitutionality but read down Section 33(2) to require judicial authorisation and restricted Section 57 (private entity authentication) as unconstitutional.

Under the RTI Act, UIDAI invokes Section 8(1)(a) (security of the state — disclosure would compromise the integrity of the biometric database), Section 8(1)(j) (personal information — biometric and demographic data of residents), and Section 8(1)(e) (fiduciary relationship — UIDAI holds data in trust for residents). The CIC, in UIDAI v. Anjali Bhardwaj (CIC/SB/C/2018/000567, decided 12 March 2019), applied a document-by-document harm test: it ordered disclosure of aggregate enrolment statistics, authentication transaction volumes, rejection rates, and grievance redressal metrics (proactive disclosure under Section 4), but upheld denial of individual enrolment records, biometric templates, and authentication logs linked to specific Aadhaar numbers. The Commission held that the Aadhaar Act’s Section 29 creates a statutory non-obstante exemption for core biometrics that prevails over the RTI Act’s public interest override under Section 8(2) — a rare instance where a special law carves out an absolute RTI exemption.

For aspirants, the analytical framework is: (1) Core biometric information (fingerprints, iris, face) = absolute exemption under Aadhaar Act Section 29 + RTI Section 8(1)(a)/(j); (2) Demographic information (name, address, DOB, gender) = personal information under Section 8(1)(j), disclosable only to the data subject (the resident) after authentication; (3) Aggregate/statistical data = mandatory proactive disclosure under Section 4 RTI Act (UIDAI publishes monthly enrolment and authentication dashboards); (4) Authentication logs = disclosable to the resident (own logs) under Section 8(1)(j) harm test; not disclosable to third parties; (5) Security audit reports, penetration test results = denied under Section 8(1)(a) (compromise database security). The Puttaswamy judgment did not bring Aadhaar data under RTI; it strengthened the statutory architecture by mandating judicial oversight for any disclosure. A frequent examiner trap: confusing the Right to Privacy (Article 21) with RTI exemptions — privacy is the constitutional foundation; Sections 8(1)(j) and 29 Aadhaar Act are the statutory implementation. They operate in tandem, not in conflict.

  • Assuming political parties are not public authorities under RTI — the CIC’s 2013 full-bench order held they are; the 2013 Amendment Bill to exclude them lapsed; no subsequent legislation has overturned the order.
  • Conflating legislative privilege (Article 105/194) with blanket RTI exemption for legislatures — only privilege-protected deliberations are exempt under Section 8(1)(c); Secretariat administration and MPLADS/MLALADS are fully subject to RTI.
  • Claiming the 2019 Subhash Chandra Agarwal judgment brought the "judiciary under RTI" — it brought the CJI's administrative office under RTI; adjudicatory deliberations and collegium minutes remain protected.
  • Treating TRAI’s citizen charter as merely aspirational — its service standards are backed by legally enforceable QoS Regulations under the TRAI Act, with financial disincentives and TDSAT as a specialised appellate forum.
  • Believing the Puttaswamy judgment opened Aadhaar data to RTI — it upheld the Aadhaar Act’s statutory exemptions (Section 29 core biometrics, Section 33 judicial oversight) and did not dilute Section 8(1)(j) or (a) applicability.
  • Overlooking the distinction between proactive disclosure (Section 4) and reactive disclosure (Section 6) for UIDAI — aggregate statistics are proactively published; individual records are denied under Section 8(1)(j)/(a) even to the data subject for core biometrics.
  • Confusing the Banking Ombudsman’s charter enforceability with TRAI’s — Banking Ombudsman awards are binding up to ₹20 lakh with High Court appeal; TDSAT orders on QoS violations are appealable only to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law.
